prompt: In many countries, fewer school leavers are choosing to study science and mathematics at a higher level. Why is this happening? What could be done to encourage more young people into these subjects?
essay:
In many education systems the proportion of students continuing with physics, chemistry and mathematics after the compulsory stage has been falling for years. I believe the causes are partly practical and partly cultural, and that any effective response has to address both.

The most obvious reason is risk. Where university admission depends on a single set of grades, students make a rational calculation: a mathematics paper that is marked strictly is a worse bet than a humanities subject in which a solid grade is easier to secure. A learner who is capable of physics but not certain of an excellent mark will often avoid it, and schools that are judged on results rarely discourage them.

A second cause is that these subjects are frequently taught as a body of content to be memorised rather than as a way of investigating things. Students who never design an experiment or model a real problem have no way of discovering that the work might suit them. There is also a persistent image problem, since the scientific careers are still widely imagined as solitary and poorly paid compared with finance or law.

Solutions therefore need to work on both fronts. Admissions systems could weight difficult subjects more generously, so that choosing physics no longer costs a candidate a place. Curricula could be rebalanced towards genuine investigation, with laboratory work and data projects given the time they need rather than squeezed in around examination preparation. Finally, sustained contact with working scientists and engineers — through school partnerships and paid summer placements — would correct the assumption that these careers are narrow or unrewarding.

In short, young people are responding sensibly to the incentives and impressions they are given, and it is those, rather than the students themselves, that need to change.
title: Why fewer school leavers study science and maths
